name: Stage 3 exit test
description: The exit test for Advanced, in four papers and four checks. The papers cover probability at interview pace, mental arithmetic, research papers and two coding problems in an hour. The checks cover Zhou's probability chapter, Zetamac, your mock interviews and your replication. Topics 3.2 and 3.4 are optional, so they sit in their own topic exams instead.

parts.name: Paper A: probability and expected value at interview pace

items.title: An even product
items.prose: Two fair dice are rolled. You are told only that the product of the faces is even.
items.question: What is the chance that their sum is even?

feedback.correct: Nine of the 27 rolls with an even product have an even sum.
feedback.generic: List the rolls the news leaves, then count those with an even sum.

byKey.ignored-news: You gave the chance before the news. An even product rules out every odd-odd roll.
byKey.whole-table: You counted the 9 even-even rolls out of all 36. Divide by the 27 rolls with an even product.

explain.text: An even product rules out the 9 odd-odd rolls, leaving 27. Given that, the sum is even only when both faces are even: 9 rolls. So the chance is $\tfrac{9}{27} = \tfrac13$.

items.title: Until a roll repeats
items.prose: Roll a fair die again and again. Stop at the first roll that shows the same face as the roll before it.
items.question: How many rolls do you expect to make, counting the last one?

feedback.correct: One roll to start, then a wait of 6 on average.
feedback.generic: The first roll cannot match. After it, what is the chance each roll matches the one before?

byKey.no-first: You counted the wait for a match but not the first roll, which has nothing to match.
byKey.one-pair: You waited for one fixed pair of faces. Any face will do, as long as it equals the one before.

explain.text: The first roll cannot match. After it, each roll matches the one before with chance $\tfrac16$, whatever came earlier. So we expect $1 + 6 = 7$ rolls.

items.title: A lead of two
items.prose: Two traders play a series of points for a bet. Ana wins each point with chance 0.6, independently. The series ends as soon as one of them leads by two points.
items.question: Two questions on the series.

parts.question: What is the chance that Ana wins the series? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Play the points in pairs: $0.36$ against $0.16$.
feedback.generic: A pair of points either ends the series or brings it back to level.

byKey.one-point: You gave the chance of one point. A lead of two favours the stronger player further.
byKey.two-straight: You counted only two wins in a row. After a split, the series is back where it started.

parts.question: How many points do you expect the series to last? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Pairs of points, each ending the series with chance 0.52.
feedback.generic: Count the expected number of pairs, then turn pairs into points.

byKey.two-points: Two points end it only when one player takes both. A split, chance 0.48, starts it again.
byKey.pairs-not-points: You counted pairs of points. Each pair is two points.

explain.text: A pair of points ends the series with chance $0.6^2 + 0.4^2 = 0.52$, and Ana takes it with $0.36$. So she wins with $0.36 / 0.52 \approx 0.6923$. The series lasts $2 / 0.52 \approx 3.8462$ points on average.

items.title: Side by side
items.prose: Ten traders, two of them desk heads, take the ten seats of a round table in a random order.
items.question: What is the chance that the two desk heads sit next to each other?

options.why: You counted 2 neighbouring seats out of 10. The first head takes a seat, so 9 are left.
You counted one neighbouring seat. At a round table everyone has two neighbours.
You fixed both heads in one pair of seats. The first head may sit anywhere.

feedback.correct: Seat the first head, then place the second.
feedback.generic: Wherever the first head sits, how many seats are left, and how many touch hers?

byKey.b: You counted 2 neighbouring seats out of 10. The first head takes a seat, so 9 are left.
byKey.c: You counted one neighbouring seat. At a round table everyone has two neighbours.
byKey.d: You fixed both heads in one pair of seats. The first head may sit anywhere.

explain.text: Seat the first head anywhere; by symmetry her seat does not matter. The second head is then equally likely to take any of the 9 other seats. Two of those touch the first head's seat, so the chance is $\tfrac29$.

items.title: A product below one half
items.prose: Draw $X$ and $Y$ independently and uniformly from $[0, 1]$.
items.question: What is $P(XY < \tfrac12)$? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: A strip of area one half, plus the area under a hyperbola.
feedback.generic: Split at $x = \tfrac12$. Left of it every $y$ works; right of it $y < \tfrac{1}{2x}$.

byKey.uniform-product: You treated $XY$ as uniform. A product of two uniforms piles up near 0.
byKey.curve-only: You kept only the curved part. For $x \le \tfrac12$ every $y$ works, which adds $\tfrac12$.

explain.text: For $x \le \tfrac12$ every $y$ works, an area of $\tfrac12$. For $x > \tfrac12$ we need $y < \tfrac{1}{2x}$, an area of $\int_{1/2}^{1} \tfrac{1}{2x}\,dx = \tfrac12 \ln 2$. So the chance is $\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 \ln 2 \approx 0.8466$.

items.title: Tight or wide
items.prose:
A market maker plays a repeated game with an arbitrageur. Each round she quotes tight or wide, and he trades or waits. Her gain per round, in £, is his loss:

| | Trade | Wait |
|---|---|---|
| Tight | 2 | −1 |
| Wide | −3 | 4 |
items.question: Two questions on her best mix.

parts.question: With what chance should she quote tight, so that his choice does not matter? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.correct: Make his two choices cost him the same.
feedback.generic: Write her average gain against Trade and against Wait, as functions of her tight share $p$.

byKey.his-mix: You made her indifferent, which fixes his mix. Her mix must make his two choices pay the same.
byKey.pure-tight: You chose her best row against Trade. A pure quote is read and exploited.

parts.question: At that mix, what does she gain per round on average, in £? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.correct: The same gain against either reply.
feedback.generic: Put her mix into either column.

byKey.pure-maximin: You gave the most she can guarantee with one pure quote. Mixing raises it.
byKey.half-half: You mixed half and half. Then he trades, and she loses £0.50 a round.

explain.text: Against Trade her tight share $p$ earns $2p - 3(1 - p)$; against Wait it earns $-p + 4(1 - p)$. Setting them equal gives $10p = 7$, so $p = 0.7$. She then gains $2(0.7) - 3(0.3) = £0.5$ a round whatever he does.

items.title: A six against a nine
items.prose: Ana and Ben take turns, Ana first. Ana rolls one die and wins on a six. Ben rolls two dice and wins on a total of 9 or more.
items.question: What is the chance that Ana wins? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Ana's chance is $\tfrac{18}{43}$.
feedback.generic: Find the chance a full round has no winner, then sum over rounds.

byKey.six-each: You gave the answer for a six on each side. Ben's total of 9 or more comes with chance $\tfrac{10}{36}$.
byKey.at-once: You weighed the two chances per turn as if they rolled at once. Ana rolls before Ben in every round.

explain.text: Ben's two dice total 9 or more in 10 of 36 rolls. A round passes with no winner with chance $\tfrac56 \cdot \tfrac{26}{36} = \tfrac{65}{108}$. So $P = \tfrac16 / (1 - \tfrac{65}{108}) = \tfrac{18}{43} \approx 0.4186$.

items.title: Wins before the third loss
items.prose: A trader takes one bet a day. Each bet wins with chance 0.6, independently. She stops for the month after her third losing bet.
items.question: How many winning bets do you expect before she stops?

feedback.correct: Three runs of wins, each with mean 1.5.
feedback.generic: Split the bets at each loss. How many wins come before one loss, on average?

byKey.all-bets: You counted every bet, the three losses too. Only the wins are asked for.
byKey.first-loss: You counted the wins before the first loss only. She stops at the third.

explain.text: Before each loss comes a run of wins with mean $\tfrac{0.6}{0.4} = 1.5$. Three losses means three such runs. So we expect $3 \times 1.5 = 4.499999999999999$ winning bets.

items.title: Everyone pays
items.prose: Two firms bid for a licence in an all-pay auction. Each pays its own bid, and only the higher bid wins. Each firm's value is private and uniform from £0 to £1 million. Both use the same increasing bidding rule.
items.question: In equilibrium, what does a firm with value £0.8 million bid, in £ millions? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The rule is $b(v) = v^2/2$.
feedback.generic: Bid as if your value were $w$: you win with chance $w$ and always pay $b(w)$.

byKey.first-price: You used the first-price bid $v/2$. Here a loser pays too, so bids are lower.
byKey.truthful: You bid your value, as in a second-price auction. In an all-pay auction that loses money on every defeat.

explain.text: Bidding as if your value were $w$ wins with chance $w$ and costs $b(w)$ for sure. So you maximise $vw - b(w)$. Truthful play needs $b'(v) = v$, so $b(v) = v^2/2$, and at $v = 0.8$ the bid is £0.32 million.

items.title: An edge over 100 bets
items.prose: You take 100 independent £1 bets at evens. Each one wins with chance 0.55.
items.question: What is the chance that you finish down overall? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Down means at most 49 wins.
feedback.generic: Count wins, with mean 55. Being down means fewer than 50 of them.

byKey.sure-profit: You treated a positive edge as a sure profit. The luck over 100 bets is as large as the £10 edge.
byKey.no-half: You cut the normal curve at exactly 50 wins. Down means at most 49, so cut at 49.5.
byKey.level-counts: You counted finishing level as down. At exactly 50 wins you are flat.

explain.text: Being down means at most 49 wins out of 100. The wins have mean 55 and sd $\sqrt{100 \times 0.55 \times 0.45} \approx 4.97$. So $P(W \le 49.5) \approx \Phi(-1.11) \approx 0.13$, and the exact binomial sum gives 0.1346.

items.title: Two models agree
items.prose: A regime break starts on 2% of days. Two models each flag 90% of break days and 5% of normal days. Given the kind of day, the two models flag independently.
items.question: Both models flag today. What is the chance that a break has started? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Square both likelihoods, then compare the weights.
feedback.generic: Weigh a break day with two flags against a normal day with two flags.

byKey.one-model: You used one model's flag. The second flag multiplies both likelihoods again.
byKey.hits-squared-only: You squared the 90% but left the 5% as it was. A normal day needs two false flags.

explain.text: A break day with two flags has weight $0.02 \times 0.9^2 = 0.0162$. A normal day with two flags has $0.98 \times 0.05^2 = 0.00245$. So the chance is $0.0162 / 0.01865 \approx 0.8686$.

items.title: A buyer who may know
items.prose: The interviewer picks a whole number $X$ from 1 to 100, each equally likely. You quote 45 bid, 55 ask on $X$. Half the time the trader knows $X$: he buys if $X > 55$, sells if $X < 45$, and otherwise does nothing. Otherwise he does not know $X$, and buys or sells with chance one half each.
items.question: Three questions on one trade.

parts.question: What is the chance that the trader buys from you? Give 3 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Add the noise buys and the informed buys.
feedback.generic: Weight each kind of trader by one half.

byKey.noise-only: You gave the noise trader's chance alone. Half the time the trader is informed.
byKey.informed-only: You gave the informed trader's chance alone. Half the time the trader buys at random.

parts.question: He buys at 55. What is your new fair value for $X$? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: A buy is news, but only partly.
feedback.generic: Weigh the noise buys, with mean 50.5, against the informed buys, with mean 78.

byKey.all-informed: You treated every buyer as informed. Half the buyers trade at random and carry no news.
byKey.no-update: You kept the prior. A buy is likelier when $X$ is high, so it moves fair value up.
byKey.equal-weights: You weighted the two kinds of buyer equally. Their weights are 0.25 and 0.225.

parts.question: On average, what is that one sale at 55 worth to you, in points? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Sale price minus the new fair value.
feedback.generic: You sold at 55 something now worth your new fair value.

byKey.sign: You gave the loss as a gain. You sold at 55 something now worth more.
byKey.prior-value: You valued the sale against the prior 50.5. The buy itself is news.

explain.text: Buys come from noise with weight $0.25$ and from informed traders with weight $0.5 \times 0.45 = 0.225$. So $E[X \mid \text{buy}] = (0.25 \times 50.5 + 0.225 \times 78) / 0.475 \approx 63.53$. The sale at 55 then loses about 8.53 on average.

parts.name: Paper B: mental arithmetic at Zetamac pace
Paper C: research papers and their traps

items.title: A history that arrives late
items.prose: A hedge fund database lets a fund start reporting whenever it likes. A fund that joins also loads its past returns. Funds tend to join after a good year.
items.question: Which bias does this put in the database's average return?

options.text: Backfill bias: the early records were chosen for being good.
Survivorship bias: dead funds have dropped out.
options.why: You named the bias from funds that close. Here funds join with a chosen past.

options.text: Look-ahead bias: returns are known before they happen.
options.why: You named a timing leak. No trade here uses data from the future.

options.text: Data snooping: many rules were tried on one sample.
options.why: You named a search over many rules. No rule was searched here.

feedback.correct: The loaded history was chosen after the fact.
feedback.generic: Ask which funds choose to join, and when.

byKey.b: You named the bias from funds that close. Here funds join with a chosen past.
byKey.c: You named a timing leak. No trade here uses data from the future.
byKey.d: You named a search over many rules. No rule was searched here.

explain.text: A fund that joins after a good run brings that run with it. So the database's early years look better than a typical fund's record. A fix is to drop each fund's returns from before its join date.

items.title: Six per cent a month
items.prose:
A colleague's momentum backtest earns 6% a month. `ret` holds monthly returns, one row a month. `rank_weights` sets +1 on winners and −1 on losers in each row.

```python
w = rank_weights(ret.rolling(6).sum())
pnl = (w * ret).sum(axis=1)
```
items.question: What is wrong?

options.text: The weights use month $t$'s return to trade month $t$.
A 6-month window is too short to rank on.
options.why: You questioned the window. Jegadeesh and Titman rank on 3 to 12 months; the bug is timing.

options.text: Summed returns should be compounded first.
options.why: You looked at sums against products. That moves a few ranks, not 6% a month.

options.text: The loser leg should be dropped.
options.why: You changed the design. Dropping losers does not explain 6% a month.

feedback.correct: Row $t$ of the weights already knows month $t$.
feedback.generic: Check which months row $t$ of the rolling sum contains.

byKey.b: You questioned the window. Jegadeesh and Titman rank on 3 to 12 months; the bug is timing.
byKey.c: You looked at sums against products. That moves a few ranks, not 6% a month.
byKey.d: You changed the design. Dropping losers does not explain 6% a month.

explain.text: Row $t$ of the rolling sum includes month $t$, and `pnl` multiplies it by month $t$ again. The book earns the returns it ranked on, which is look-ahead. Use `w.shift(1)`, so month $t$ trades on weights set at the end of month $t - 1$.

items.title: Only the funds still open
items.prose: A database follows 200 funds through one year. 40 close during the year, with an average return of −15% up to closing. The 160 that survive average 9%. The database keeps only the funds still open at the year end.
items.question: By how many percentage points does it overstate the average fund's return? Give 1 decimal place.

feedback.correct: Survivors' 9% against a true 4.2%.
feedback.generic: Weight the two groups by their numbers of funds, then compare with 9%.

byKey.true-mean: You gave the true average. The question asks for the gap from the reported 9%.
byKey.equal-groups: You averaged the two groups equally. Weight them by 160 and 40 funds.

explain.text: The true average weights both groups: $0.8 \times 9\% + 0.2 \times (-15\%) = 4.2\%$. The database reports the survivors' 9%. So it overstates by $9 - 4.2 = 4.8$ points.

items.title: Book equity in June
items.prose: Fama and French (1993) form portfolios at the end of June of year $t$. They use book equity from the fiscal year ending in calendar year $t - 1$. A firm's fiscal year ends in March.
items.question: You form portfolios at the end of June 2015 by their rule. Which year's book equity does the firm contribute?

options.text: The year ending March 2014
The year ending March 2015
options.why: You took the latest year end. The rule uses the year ending in 2014, so the accounts are surely out.

options.text: The year ending December 2014
options.why: You used a calendar year. This firm's years end in March.

options.text: The year ending March 2016
options.why: You used accounts from after June 2015. That is look-ahead.

feedback.correct: The fiscal year ending in calendar 2014.
feedback.generic: Find calendar year $t - 1$, then the firm's year end inside it.

byKey.b: You took the latest year end. The rule uses the year ending in 2014, so the accounts are surely out.
byKey.c: You used a calendar year. This firm's years end in March.
byKey.d: You used accounts from after June 2015. That is look-ahead.

explain.text: Here $t - 1 = 2014$, and the firm's fiscal year in 2014 ends in March. The rule leaves at least six months between a year end and its use. That gap makes sure the accounts were public by June 2015.

items.title: What January 2010 knew
items.prose: A replication plan lists six choices for a test that starts trading in January 2010.
items.question: Select all that apply: which choices use information that was not available in January 2010?

options.text: Scale 2009 returns by each share's volatility over 1990 to 2024.
Pick the holding period with the best Sharpe ratio over 1990 to 2024.
Trade only shares in the 2024 index, all the way back to 2010.
Choose pairs by their distance over 2009 only.
options.why: You flagged a formation window. All of 2009 was known by January 2010.

options.text: Use book equity from fiscal years ending in 2008.
options.why: You flagged old accounts. Fiscal 2008 accounts were public by 2010.

options.text: Charge costs at the average 2009 bid-ask spread.
options.why: You flagged a cost estimate. The 2009 spread was known before 2010.

feedback.correct: Three choices reach past 2009.
feedback.generic: For each choice, find the latest date whose data it needs.

explain.text: The full-sample volatility, the holding period chosen on 1990 to 2024 and the 2024 index all use the future. The pairs window, the 2008 accounts and the 2009 spread were all known by then. Each leaked choice flatters the backtest.

items.title: A test on later years
items.prose: Gatev, Goetzmann and Rouwenhorst (2006) report pairs returns to 2002. You plan to test their method on 2003 to 2024.
items.question: Put the steps in order. Leave out the two that do not belong.

lines.text: Write down the paper's rules: 12 months of formation, 6 of trading, open at 2 sd.
Reproduce the paper's main table on its own years.
Freeze the code and the rules in a tagged commit.
Run the frozen code once on 2003 to 2024.
Report what share of the paper's return survived.
Tune the opening threshold on 2003 to 2024 until it matches the paper.
lines.why: You tuned on the held-out years. Then they no longer test anything.

lines.text: Drop the years in which the method lost money.
lines.why: You removed the bad years. That hides what the test should show.

feedback.correct: Fix, match, freeze, run once, report.
feedback.generic: The held-out years may be used only once, after the code is frozen.

byKey.x1: You tuned on the held-out years. Then they no longer test anything.
byKey.x2: You removed the bad years. That hides what the test should show.
byKey.left-out: A step that belongs is missing. Each of rules, match, freeze, run and report is needed.

explain.text: Fix the rules first and prove the code by matching the paper. Freeze it, then spend the held-out years once. Tuning on them, or dropping years, turns the test back into a fit.

items.title: What costs leave
items.prose: A momentum book earns 1.1% a month before costs, per £1 long and £1 short. Each month it buys and sells shares worth £1.40 in all.
items.question: What cost per £1 traded wipes out the return? Give it in % to 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Costs fall on the £1.40 traded each month.
feedback.generic: Set the monthly cost, £1.40 times the rate, equal to the 1.1% earned.

byKey.twice: You charged each trade twice. The £1.40 already counts buys and sells.
byKey.no-turnover: You charged costs on the position, not on what is traded. Only the £1.40 traded pays.

explain.text: Costs are charged on what is traded: $1.4c$ a month. They wipe out the 1.1% when $1.4c = 1.1\%$. So $c = 1.1\% / 1.4 \approx 0.79\%$ per £1 traded.

items.title: A bar of three
items.prose: A new factor earns 0.45% a month, with sd 3.1%, over 360 months. The months are close to independent.
items.question: Two questions on the evidence.

parts.question: What is its $t$ statistic? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Mean over its standard error.
feedback.generic: Divide the sd by $\sqrt{360}$, then divide the mean by that.

byKey.no-root: You divided by the sd, not the standard error. Divide the sd by $\sqrt{360}$ first.
byKey.years: You counted years, not months. There are 360 monthly returns.

parts.question: Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016) say a new factor should clear $t = 3$. What should the note say?

options.text: It clears 2 but not 3, so call it unproven.
It clears 2, so it is a real factor.
options.why: You used the single-test bar of 2. After hundreds of factors were tried, 3 is safer.

options.text: It fails 3, so the factor has no effect.
options.why: You read a miss as proof of zero. A $t$ of 2.75 is weak evidence, not none.

options.text: Annualise first, since $t$ grows with the horizon.
options.why: You changed units. A $t$ statistic is the same in monthly or annual terms.

feedback.correct: Promising, not proven.
feedback.generic: Compare the $t$ with both bars.

byKey.b: You used the single-test bar of 2. After hundreds of factors were tried, 3 is safer.
byKey.c: You read a miss as proof of zero. A $t$ of 2.75 is weak evidence, not none.
byKey.d: You changed units. A $t$ statistic is the same in monthly or annual terms.

explain.text: The standard error is $3.1 / \sqrt{360} \approx 0.163$, so $t \approx 2.75$. That clears 2 but not the bar of 3 that Harvey, Liu and Zhu set for new factors. The note should call it promising but unproven.

items.title: One small share
items.prose: In one month a loser decile holds ten shares. Nine are worth £5 billion each and return 1%. The tenth is worth £0.05 billion and returns 60%.
items.question: Two figures for the month.

parts.question: What is the decile's equal-weighted return? Give it in % to 1 decimal place.

feedback.correct: Each share counts one tenth.
feedback.generic: Average the ten returns, each with weight one tenth.

byKey.big-only: You gave the nine large shares alone. The tenth share counts one tenth too.
byKey.value-weighted: You weighted by size. Equal weights give the small share a tenth of the decile.

parts.question: What is its value-weighted return? Give it in % to 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Weights by size: £45 billion against £0.05 billion.
feedback.generic: Weight each return by the share's value, then divide by the decile's total value.

byKey.equal-weighted: You gave each share a tenth. Weight by value instead.
byKey.big-only: You left the small share out. It still adds $0.05 \times 60\%$ to the total.

explain.text: Equal weights give $(9 \times 1\% + 60\%) / 10 = 6.9\%$. Value weights give $(45 \times 1\% + 0.05 \times 60\%) / 45.05 \approx 1.07\%$. One tiny share drives the equal-weighted figure, so a replication reports both weightings.

items.title: One plain sentence
items.prose: Your replication of a value strategy matches the paper on its years: 0.84% a month, $t = 3.2$. On the 15 years since publication it earns 0.21% a month, $t = 0.7$.
items.question: Which sentence belongs in the note?

options.text: A quarter of the effect survived, too little to tell from zero.
Three quarters of the effect survived publication.
options.why: You gave the share lost, $1 - 0.25$. The share kept is $0.21 / 0.84$.

options.text: The effect is gone, so it was never real.
options.why: You read a weak $t$ as proof. The in-sample match also stands.

options.text: The effect survived, since 0.21% is still positive.
options.why: You ignored the noise. With $t = 0.7$, 0.21% cannot be told from zero.

feedback.correct: A quarter kept, and within noise of zero.
feedback.generic: Divide the later mean by the earlier one, then read the later $t$.

byKey.b: You gave the share lost, $1 - 0.25$. The share kept is $0.21 / 0.84$.
byKey.c: You read a weak $t$ as proof. The in-sample match also stands.
byKey.d: You ignored the noise. With $t = 0.7$, 0.21% cannot be told from zero.

explain.text: The kept share is $0.21 / 0.84 = 25\%$. With $t = 0.7$ the later mean is within noise of zero. A plain note says both, without calling the effect gone or intact.

items.title: Is it just reversal?
items.prose: A pairs strategy earns 0.90% a month. Regressed on a short-term reversal factor, its beta is 0.35. The factor earns 1.40% a month over the same years.
items.question: What is the pairs strategy's alpha, in % a month? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Subtract beta times the factor's return.
feedback.generic: Find how much of the 0.90% the factor explains, then take it away.

byKey.whole-factor: You subtracted the whole factor return. Only the beta share, $0.35 \times 1.40\%$, is explained.
byKey.scaled-own: You scaled the strategy's own return by the beta. Alpha subtracts beta times the factor's return.

explain.text: The factor explains $0.35 \times 1.40\% = 0.49\%$ a month. What is left is the alpha, $0.90\% - 0.49\% = 0.41\%$. So a little over half the return is reversal exposure.

items.title: The best of twenty
items.prose: You try 20 independent variants of a rule on 5 years of data. None has any edge. Each variant's annual Sharpe ratio estimate is then normal, with mean 0 and sd $1/\sqrt{5}$.
items.question: What is the chance that the best of the 20 shows a Sharpe ratio above 1? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: One minus the chance that all 20 stay below 1.
feedback.generic: Find the chance one variant beats 1, then the chance that none of the 20 does.

byKey.one-variant: You gave the chance for one variant. The best of 20 has 20 tries at it.
byKey.added-chances: You added the 20 chances, which counts overlaps twice. Use $1 - (1 - p)^{20}$.

explain.text: One variant beats 1 with chance $1 - \Phi(\sqrt5) \approx 0.0127$. All 20 stay below with $(1 - 0.0127)^{20} \approx 0.775$. So the best clears 1 with chance about 0.23, though no variant has an edge.

items.title: False factors among the passes
items.prose: Suppose 300 candidate factors are tested. 200 have no effect. The other 100 are real, each with an expected $t$ of 3.5. Treat each $t$ as normal with sd 1. A factor passes when its $t$ is above the bar.
items.question: Two questions on the false share.

parts.question: With a bar of $t > 2$, what share of the factors that pass are false? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: 4.55 false passes against 93.32 real ones.
feedback.generic: Count the expected null passes and real passes, then take the false share.

byKey.over-tested: You divided by all 300 tested. Divide by the number that pass.
byKey.null-rate: You gave the chance that one null factor passes. The share also needs the real passes.

parts.question: With a bar of $t > 3$, what is that share? Give 4 decimal places.

feedback.correct: 0.27 false passes against 69.15 real ones.
feedback.generic: Repeat the count with the bar at 3.

byKey.null-rate: You gave the chance that one null factor passes. The share also needs the real passes.
byKey.over-tested: You divided by all 300 tested. Divide by the number that pass.

explain.text: At $t > 2$, $200 \times 0.0228 \approx 4.55$ null factors pass beside $100 \times \Phi(1.5) \approx 93.32$ real ones, a false share of 0.0465. At $t > 3$ the nulls fall to 0.27 and the real ones to 69.15, a share of 0.0039. The higher bar costs a quarter of the real factors but almost removes the false ones.

items.title: What the desk could see
items.prose: A point-in-time join stops a backtest from using accounts before they were public. Each report is a tuple `(ticker, period_end, published, value)` with ISO date strings such as `'2015-03-20'`. A later report may restate an earlier period.
items.question: Write `as_of(reports, date)`, a dict from ticker to the value known on `date`. Use only reports published on or before `date`. Per ticker, take the latest `period_end`, and for a restated period the latest `published`. Leave out tickers with nothing published yet.

widget.how: Check runs 7 hidden tests. Each compares your dict with the expected one exactly.

feedback.correct: Filter on the publication date, then keep the latest period per ticker.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Open the first one that failed below the editor.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Read the first line of the message under the editor.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 asks for 31 December 2015. BBB's restatement, published in September, replaces its June figure.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 is the day AAA's 2015 accounts come out. On or before `date` includes that day.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 restates an old period after a newer one is out. The latest `period_end` still wins.

explain.text: Filter on `published <= date` first: that is the look-ahead guard. Then keep, per ticker, the largest `(period_end, published)` pair. ISO date strings sort in date order, so plain string comparison works.

items.title: A fair test after publication
items.prose: A paper reports $t = 4.0$ for a strategy over 240 months. Suppose half its mean return survives publication, with the same volatility. You will test it on the 120 months since.
items.question: Three questions on the test.

parts.question: What $t$ statistic do you expect out of sample? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: Half the mean, and a standard error $\sqrt2$ times larger.
feedback.generic: $t$ scales with the mean and with the square root of the months.

byKey.halved-only: You halved the mean but kept 240 months. With 120 months the standard error is $\sqrt2$ times larger.
byKey.full-mean: You shortened the sample but kept the full mean. Only half the mean survives.

parts.question: Treat the out-of-sample $t$ as normal with that mean and sd 1. What is the chance that it exceeds 2? Give 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Standardise 2 against the expected $t$ from the first part.

byKey.nothing-survived: You used a mean of 0, as if nothing survived. Centre on 1.41.
byKey.below-two: You gave the chance that $t$ falls below 2. The question asks for above.

parts.question: How many months would give an expected out-of-sample $t$ of 2?

feedback.correct: Solve $2\sqrt{n/240} = 2$.
feedback.generic: With half the mean, the expected $t$ is $2\sqrt{n/240}$.

byKey.same-t: You aimed for the paper's $t$ of 4. A $t$ of 2 needs a quarter of those months.
byKey.doubled: You doubled the months for half the mean. $t$ grows with $\sqrt n$, so check the square.

explain.text: Halving the mean halves $t$, and half the months divides it by $\sqrt2$: $4 \times 0.5 / \sqrt2 \approx 1.41$. So $t$ tops 2 only about 28\% of the time, though half the effect is real. An expected $t$ of 2 needs 240 months.
